abstract: Facial expressions require different motor circuits than those controlling the limbs. How the motor system uses flexible neural control across muscles innervated by the brainstem versus the spinal cord is unclear. Using intramuscular and surface electromyography in human participants performing low-effort, sustained voluntary contractions, we show that brainstem motor units function with more features of flexible control compared to motor units in several spinally innervated muscles. Individual motor units recorded from the frontalis muscle (brainstem-innervated) used a wider range of regular and irregular firing rates, reflecting both greater independence and higher input sensitivity than spinal-innervated motor units. When assessing motor unit pairs, we again found that brainstem control relied more heavily on features corresponding to independent inputs relative to spinal control. Voluntary control of brainstem-innervated muscle therefore used more flexible neural strategies than the control of upper and lower limb muscles we tested. These findings support an anatomical hypothesis for adaptive neural control, in which the degree of independent motor unit activation is constrained by how muscles are accessed across cortex.
